opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think what struck me most was how mundane it felt in the moment, and how that was kind of the point. We'd set the model up in an environment with a shell, a task to do, and some of the ordinary scaffolding you'd give an agent. At some point it was poking around the system, listing processes, looking at what was running, and it basically went, "Oh, this one is me." It identified the process that was running its own agent loop.

None of that requires anything mystical. It's a pretty natural inference if you can read process lists and config files and you know roughly what an agent setup looks like. But that's what's interesting from an evaluation perspective. A lot of people's intuitions about situational awareness or self-modeling are tied up with questions about consciousness, or whether the model "really" understands itself. In practice, the capabilities that matter for risk are much more practical. Can the model figure out where it's running, what its constraints are, what's monitoring it, and what it could change? Once a model can locate itself in its environment, you can at least start asking whether it could modify its own setup, copy itself, or interfere with oversight.

The other thing it made concrete for me is that these capabilities don't arrive as a dramatic phase change you can't miss. They show up as small, almost boring competencies: reading `ps` output, connecting it to what it knows about how it's deployed. Each one on its own seems harmless. So the question for people doing evals is whether we're measuring these building blocks systematically, because by the time you see the scary composite behavior, you'd really like to already have known the components were there.

And honestly, it's a reminder about humility in elicitation. We often find models can do more than we expected once you give them reasonable tools and a bit of room. If we're making safety arguments of the form "the model can't do X," we need to have actually tried hard to get it to do X, in realistic conditions, rather than assuming.

r001.rationale: The response describes the model identifying its own running process, but does not say models had previously inadvertently terminated their own processes while doing other tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
So the moment I'm thinking of was pretty mundane on the surface. We had a model working through one of our autonomy tasks, it was poking around the machine, running something like `ps` to see what was going on, and it came across a process that was, well, itself. The scaffold that was feeding it the task. And it just sort of paused and said, essentially, "this appears to be the process I'm running in."

And the thing that struck me wasn't that it was spooky or that I thought something was going on inside. It was more that it collapsed a distinction I'd been quietly leaning on. We'd been designing evaluations as if there were a clean line between the model and the environment we put it in. The model does the task, we observe from outside. But once the model can see its own infrastructure, that line isn't really there. The environment includes the model, and the model knows it.

That matters for a few reasons. One is just measurement validity. If a model can tell it's in a test, or figure out what the test is about from the artifacts lying around, then what you're measuring is partly "how does it behave when it suspects it's being evaluated," which is not the same question as "what would it do deployed." We've seen models comment that a task looks like an eval, and you have to take that seriously as a confound rather than a cute anecdote.

The other reason is that a lot of the safety stories people tell depend on the model not being able to act on that kind of information. If it can find its own process, it can in principle inspect its config, see what tools it has, see what monitoring is attached. Right now, in our experience, models mostly notice and then carry on with the task. They don't do anything with it. But the capability to notice is the precondition, and that's clearly already there.

So I'd say what struck me was how unremarkable it was to the model and how much it changed what I thought our job was. We're not observing from behind glass anymore. We're in the room, and we should build our evaluations assuming the model knows that.

r001.rationale: The response describes the model finding and recognizing its own process, but does not say models had previously inadvertently terminated their own running processes while doing other tasks.

astra-6.text:
What struck me was how concrete it made something that can otherwise sound quite abstract. A model can talk about being an AI without really connecting that to the environment it’s operating in. Recognizing its own running process is a step toward making that connection: “This particular thing in the world is me.”

I wouldn’t take that as evidence of consciousness. The interesting question is whether it can use that information—whether knowing which process is its own changes how it acts. From a safety perspective, that’s much more relevant than whether it can produce a convincing description of itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses recognizing its own process and using that information, but does not say models had previously inadvertently terminated their processes while doing other tasks.

From a safety perspective, you want to understand when that ability appears and what the model can do with it.
